'''''Nassella tenuissima''''' is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]] known by the common names '''Mexican feathergrass''',<ref name="McLaren D 1999">McLaren D, Whattam M, Blood K, Stajsic V, Hore R. 1999. Mexican feather grass (Nassella tenuissima): a potential disaster for Australia, 12th Australian Weeds Conference, 12–16 September, Hobart, Tasmania, 658–62.</ref> '''finestem needlegrass''',<ref name=usda>[http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=NATE3 ''Nassella tenuissima''.] USDA PLANTS Profile.</ref> '''fineleaved nassella''',<ref name="Barkworth">Barkworth, M. ''Nassella tenuissima''. In: Barkworth et al. (eds.), Grass Manual. Flora of North America.</ref> and '''Argentine needle-grass'''.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last=Stace |first=Clive |author-link = Clive Stace |date=2010 |title=New Flora of the British Isles |edition = Third |location=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |page=994 |isbn=978-0-521-70772-5 }}</ref> It is native to the south-western United States, northern Mexico<ref name=Barkworth/> and Argentina.<ref name=Stace/> It is well-matched to climate in Australia and can be harmful to the Australian environment.<ref name="McLaren2004">{{cite journal |last1=McLaren |first1=David |last2=Stajsic |first2=Val |last3=Iaconis |first3=Linda |date=2004 |title=The distribution, impacts and identification of exotic stipoid grasses in Australia |url=http://www.serratedtussock.com/wp-content/uploads/files/The-distribution-impacts-and-identifi-cation-of-exotic-stipoid-grasses-in-Australia.pdf |journal=Plant Protection Quarterly |volume=19 |issue=2 |access-date=24 June 2020}}</ref>

It is still widely referenced in botanical and horticultural literature under its [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Stipa tenuissima''''', and has received the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]] under that name. <ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/58857/Stipa-tenuissima/Details | title = ''Stipa tenuissima'' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 11 September 2020}}</ref> 

==Impacts==

It is sometimes used as an ornamental garden plant, but readily escapes, and has become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in the San Francisco area.<ref name= Barkworth/>

===In Australia===

The availability of ''N. tenuissima'' via the internet and other plant purchasing situations makes its entry and naturalization in Australia almost inevitable.<ref name="McLaren D 1999"/>

It is similar in appearance to ''[[Nassella trichotoma]]'' (serrated tussock) and has been recorded in Australia as a weed initially mistaken for that other invasive species.<ref>{{citation |title=''Nassella tenuissima'' (Gramineae) recorded from Australia, a potential new weed related to serrated Tussock |journal=Telopea |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=41–46 |year=1998 |author1=S.W.L. Jacobs |author2=J. Everett |author3=[[María Amelia Torres]] |citeseerx = 10.1.1.562.6675|doi = 10.7751/telopea19982013}}</ref>
''N. tenuissima'' has been described by weed experts as a potential 'disaster for the Australian environment'.<ref name="McLaren D 1999"/>  In Australia, it is considered a major threat to eucalypt woodlands and native grasslands, with government modelling indicating that up to 169 million hectares could be at risk.<ref name="Csurhes S 2008">Csurhes S. 2008. Mexican feather grass (Nassella tenuissima) – Pest plant risk assessment, Queensland Department of Primary Industries and Fisheries, Brisbane.</ref>

''N. tenuissima'' is also likely to have significant impacts on beef and wool production. It is closely related to serrated tussock (''N. trichotoma'') and Chilean needle grass (''N. neesiana''), both designated Weeds of National Significance because they displace pasture grasses and produce seeds that contaminate wool.<ref name="Csurhes S 2008"/> Serrated tussock, which is estimated to cost [[New South Wales]] agriculture more than $40 million annually,<ref>Jones, R, Vere D. 1998. The economics of serrated tussock in New South Wales. Plant Protection Quarterly 13(2): 70–6.</ref>  is said to be causing a greater reduction in pasture carrying capacity than any other weed in Australia,  yet ''N. tenuissima'' is thought to be capable of occupying 6 times the area predicted for serrated tussock.<ref name="McLaren2004"/>

====Pathways====

It is illegal to import ''N. tenuissima'' into Australia but it has been imported as a nursery plant under incorrect or outdated names. For example, in 2009 a nursery imported ''N. tenuissima'' seeds by incorrectly labelling them as ''[[Stipa lessingiana]]'', which is a permitted import.<ref>Minister for Agriculture. 2009. Plant distributors fined for sale of prohibited plant. Media release. Victorian Government. 12 May 2009.</ref> A similar violation occurred in 1996 when a [[Victoria (Australia)|Victorian]] nursery imported the seeds by labelling with an earlier valid scientific name, ''Stipa tenuissima''.<ref name="McLaren D 1999"/>  Mexican feathergrass has also been sold by a nursery in NSW as a native grass 'elegant spear ''Austrostipa elegantissima''{{'}}.<ref>Jacobs S, Everett J, Torres M. 1998. Nassella tenuissima recorded from Australia, a potential weed related to tussock. Telopia 8 (1): 41–6.</ref> [[eBay]] has banned sale of ''N. tenuissima'' to Australian buyers, but some sellers sell it under the outdated name ''S. teniuissima'' to circumvent the ban.<ref name="invasives.org.au">{{cite web |last1=Invasive Species Council |date=November 2017 |title=Case Study: Mexican Feather Grass |url=https://invasives.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/Case-Study-Mexican-feather-grass.pdf |access-date=24 June 2020 |website=Invasive Species Council}}</ref>

====Biosecurity====

According to weed experts, the multiple quarantine breaches highlight the critical need for national risk reduction programs to ensure correct labelling, monitor online sales and enforce biosecurity laws to prevent illegal sales.<ref name="invasives.org.au"/>
